newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.N. reform needed to reflect reality, says Kinkel.
newsitem.headline: U.N. reform needed to reflect reality, says Kinkel.

text.p: Giving Germany a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council would bring the world body up to date with economic and political reality, Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Friday.

Under the headline "Our contribution is wanted", Kinkel wrote in a column in the Berliner Morgenpost daily that Germany was striving for permanent membership of the Council and said a seat would reward the country for its financial contribution.

"We are -- after the U.S. and Japan -- the third biggest contributor to the U.N. budget. Our financial contribution corresponds to our economic and political weight. This should guarantee our right to decision making in the highest U.N. body," he said.

"No member of the United Nations doubts that the structure of the Security Council no longer corresponds to the real geopolitical powers in the world today. The current permanent members of the Security Council reflect the world situation as it was after the end of World War Two," he told the paper.

Many states at the 185-nation annual assembly have supported bids by both countries to win powerful, veto-carrying seats on the Security Council, joining the United States, Russia, China, France and Britain which took their positions in 1945 as the victors in the war.
Members believe this would recognise their status as economic superpowers and increasing involvement in such areas as peacekeeping.
On Wednesay U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Edward Gnehm said his country would not agree to expand the Council unless Germany and Japan were given permanent seats.

Chairman of the German parliamentary U.N. sub-committee Christian Rueck welcomed Gnehm's statement and told Reuters he thought the United States had done the right thing by speaking publicly on the issue.
"We are quite happy about this proposal from the U.S. concerning Germany and Japan, though we were not expecting it."

Rueck said he hoped that bringing the discussion into the open would speed up a decision on reform, on the table now for three years. A U.N. working group has reached consensus on an unspecified increase in the size of the 15-nation body but has still not agreed how this should be done.
"I think it will initiate a further discussion. Now they might discuss it publicly," Rueck said. "I am happy there is now a formal debate about an issue that has to be resolved."
Kinkel told the Berlin daily that reform should also include the interests of developing countries which are not currently represented on the Security Council.
Germany and Japan have been at pains to stress they are now responsible members of the world community and have put the stigma of World War Two behind them.

Kinkel told the U.N. General Assembly last month: "This, the principal guardian of world peace, still bears the countenance of the year 1945 but it now needs a new one for the year 2000. It is a question of enhancing that body's legitimacy, credibility and effectiveness."

The council comprises five permanent members and 10 non-permanent members who serve two years. Among unresolved issues are whether any new permanent seats should be added, and if so, whether they should also carry the power of veto.
Gnehm said the United States would accept a modest expansion of the council beyond permanent seats for Germany and Japan, but the total should not exceed about 20 seats.
